entities.notes: Audit canonical ID. Do not confuse with Chess Records pressing-plant infrastructure records (MUSIC-001) or the 2120 S. Michigan building (a separate entity in this dossier).
entities.one_line: Chicago independent record label founded 1950 by Leonard and Phil Chess; central institution of Chicago blues, early rock and roll, and 1960s soul.

entities.notes: Broven: 'the dynamo behind Chess Records'. Died months after the GRT sale.
entities.one_line: Co-founder of Chess Records; Polish-Jewish immigrant; nightclub owner turned record executive; the label's talent scout, deal-maker and public face.

entities.notes: WWII Army veteran. Left the label after the GRT sale to run WVON; retired 1972, moved to Arizona. Blues Hall of Fame 1995.
entities.one_line: Co-founder of Chess Records; Leonard's younger brother; handled the company's business operations.

entities.notes: Ownership mechanics disputed in detail: partnership of Leonard Chess, Phil Chess and Evelyn Aron per the Chicago Landmark report (Phil full-time Jan 1950, Aron withdrew); Donald Clarke reports a 1948 buyout.
entities.one_line: Chicago label founded 1947; the company Leonard and Phil Chess bought into and renamed Chess Records in 1950.

entities.canonical_name: 2120 S. Michigan Avenue (Chess Records office and studio)
entities.notes: Organization and building are separate entities (audit rule). Erected 1911 by Matson Hill, architect Horatio R. Wilson; remodeled 1956–57 by John S. Townsend Jr., $20,000.
entities.one_line: Chess Records headquarters and studio 1957–1967; Chicago Landmark since 1990; home of Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation since 1997.

entities.notes: Organization and building are separate entities.
entities.one_line: Chess Records' eight-story final headquarters from late 1966/early 1967; integrated pressing plant, Ter-Mar Studios, shipping and label printing.
entities.subtype: commercial building / recording studio / pressing plant

entities.notes: 'Ter-Mar' = anagram of Terry and Marshall (sons of Phil and Leonard Chess). Operated at 320 E. 21st until the studio's 1979 closure.
entities.one_line: Chess's in-house studio, first at 2120 S. Michigan then at 320 E. 21st; successor to Sheldon Recording Studio.

entities.notes: Designed by audio engineer and business partner Jack Weiner (also rendered 'Jack Sheldon Wiener'); Weiner left in 1959 and Chess took control in 1958 per the Chicago Landmark report. Specialist discography (friktech, citing Billboard June 1958) dates the Ter-Mar rename to late spring 1958.
entities.one_line: Separate subsidiary initially managing the 2120 S. Michigan studio (late 1957); taken over by Chess in 1958.

entities.notes: Founding year not deeply corroborated in this pass; BMI affiliation per Wikipedia.
entities.one_line: Chess Records' publishing arm, set up 1953 by Leonard Chess and Gene Goodman; defendant in the 1977 Dixon/Waters royalty suits; plaintiff in the 1972 Led Zeppelin suit.
Chess subsidiary started 1952 as an alternate imprint for radio play; home of Bo Diddley's records.

entities.notes: Released Ramsey Lewis Trio, Ray Bryant, Wes Montgomery.
entities.one_line: Jazz and pop subsidiary: launched Dec 1955 as Marterry (from Marshall + Terry), renamed Argo, then Cadet in 1965 to avoid confusion with a British spoken-word label.

entities.notes: Ceased operations 1979.
entities.one_line: Sunnyvale, California tape company founded 1965 by Alan J. Bayley; bought Chess Records in 1969 for $6.5 million plus 20,000 shares of GRT stock.

entities.notes: Acquisition year and exact seller disputed (1985 vs 1986; All Platinum vs Sugar Hill Records Ltd.). MCA later merged into the UMG lineage.
entities.one_line: Acquired the Chess catalog rights in 1985/86 from the Robinsons' All Platinum/Sugar Hill companies.

entities.notes: MCA + PolyGram merged into UMG (1999). Keep precise: UMG owns the catalog; Geffen/UMe manages reissues.
entities.one_line: Current owner of the Chess catalog via the MCA lineage; managed by Geffen Records/Universal Music Enterprises for reissues.

Bassist, songwriter, arranger and producer; Chess's 'right arm' and creative director of its blues sessions from the early 1950s; founder of the Blues Heaven Foundation (1984) and Hoochie Coochie Music.

entities.notes: Co-plaintiff with Dixon in the 1977 Arc Music royalty suit.
entities.one_line: Flagship Chess blues artist from the 1947 Aristocrat sessions onward; 'the premier Chess blues artist during the entire existence of the label' (Chicago Landmark report).
Chess blues artist sourced via Sam Phillips in Memphis; co-credited in the 1972 'Lemon Song' settlement ($45,123 cheque, Dec 1972).

entities.notes: 'My Ding-A-Ling' (1972) was Chess's only #1 pop record.
entities.one_line: St. Louis guitarist discovered for Chess in 1955; 'Maybellene' made him the label's rock-and-roll standard-bearer; his 1958 'Johnny B. Goode' rides the Voyager Golden Record.
Chess/Checker artist from 1955; 'I'm a Man' and the 'Bo Diddley beat'; brought to Chess by Willie Dixon after being spotted street-performing on Chicago's South Side.
Chess artist from 1960 ('At Last' recorded at 2120); center of the label's 1960s soul and R&B expansion.
Harmonica virtuoso; Chess artist whose amplified harp defined the 1950s Chicago blues sound.
Harmonica player and songwriter; his Dixon-written 'Bring It On Home' (1966) was the subject of Arc Music's suit against Led Zeppelin.
Chess blues artist of the 1960s ('Wang Dang Doodle').
Blues guitarist; Chess artist retained in the late-1950s blues roster; session guitarist.
West Side blues guitarist; among the blues artists retained by Chess in the late 1950s.
Memphis producer and Sun Records founder who supplied Chess with early recordings: Howlin' Wolf, Rufus Thomas, Doctor Ross, and 'Rocket 88.'

entities.notes: Also WSDM-FM. Detailed radio history belongs to CTL-DR-BMI-002's radio track.
entities.one_line: Chicago Black-appeal radio station part-owned by the Chess brothers (launched 1963 per the Chicago Landmark report); Phil Chess ran it after the GRT sale.
Nonprofit founded 1984 by Willie Dixon to preserve blues heritage and recover royalties for exploited musicians; headquartered at 2120 S. Michigan since 1997.

entities.notes: The HistoryMakers oral-history finding aid is the primary-adjacent source.
entities.one_line: Willie Dixon's widow; purchased the 2120 S. Michigan building in 1993 and established the Blues Heaven Foundation museum there (opened 1997); foundation president.
Leonard Chess's son; Chess Records vice president (Jan–Oct 1969) and president after the GRT acquisition; later founder of Rolling Stones Records.

entities.notes: Partnered with Leonard and Phil Chess in Aristocrat per the Chicago Landmark report; introduced to Leonard via Chicago poker circles per the Chess saga documentary.
entities.one_line: Investor in Aristocrat Records and office manager; withdrew in January 1950 to establish her own distributing company.

entities.address: 3905 South Cottage Grove, Chicago (Chicago Landmark report gives 3905 South Drexel Boulevard — street-name discrepancy recorded)
entities.notes: Liquor license granted to Phil Chess Feb 1946. Andrew Tibbs of the house band was the singer whose session led Leonard into recording.
entities.one_line: After-hours South Side club owned by Leonard Chess 1946–1950; the Chess brothers' training ground before the record business; burned down October 1950.
South Michigan Avenue concentration of Black-music labels — Chess at 2120, Vee-Jay at 2129 and 1449 — within blocks of each other, 1950s–1960s.

entities.notes: Label-sleeve chronology documents All Platinum Chess reissues 1975–77.
entities.one_line: Joe and Sylvia Robinson's company; bought what remained of Chess from GRT circa 1975 and reissued the catalog (1975–77) before financial difficulty led to the MCA acquisition.

entities.notes: The All Platinum vs Sugar Hill seller attribution is the disputed hinge of the catalog chain (see red-team).
entities.one_line: Robinson-family company that issued Chess reissues; named by some accounts as the seller of the Chess masters to MCA.
British rock band sued by Arc Music (1972) and by Willie Dixon personally (1985) over Dixon compositions; both suits settled out of court (the 1985 suit in 1987).

Chess's UK subsidiary established 1969, distributed by Pye Records; a joint venture with the Middle Earth Club, London; specialized in psychedelic rock; closed 1970 after four albums and about a dozen singles.

entities.notes: Hire date conflict adjudicated in §26.
entities.one_line: A&R director at Chess (hired 1958 per the Chicago Landmark report; 1960 per Wikipedia — hire date disputed); recreated the informal nightclub atmosphere in the studio; previously scouted for King Records.
Session drummer in the Chess house band (1960s); later founder and leader of Earth, Wind & Fire.
Master recording engineer hired by Chess in 1958 after Universal Recording; defined the early 2120 studio sound; left for California 1959.
Recording engineer who replaced Chisholm in 1959; built the dual echo chambers in the 2120 basement.
Chess's A&R manager and chief producer for soul and R&B in the 1960s; had worked with Berry Gordy on early Motown songs.
Shreveport, Louisiana record distributor; in 1954 entered a production deal with Chess for Louisiana Hayride artists issued in the special 4858 series.

entities.notes: Also rendered 'Jack Sheldon Wiener' (friktech, citing Billboard).
entities.one_line: Audio engineer and business partner who designed the 2120 studio and co-owned Sheldon Recording Studios; left in 1958–59.

entities.notes: Thinly documented in this pass; do not confuse with Benny Goodman.
entities.one_line: Co-founder with Leonard Chess of Arc Music (BMI), 1953.
GRT's label into which Chess was consolidated by 1972; a 1969 joint venture with Pye Records that GRT bought out in 1972.

entities.canonical_name: Sammy Dyer School of the Theater
entities.one_line: Long-established South Side theater and dance school that occupied 2120 S. Michigan from 1969.
Former Chess session guitarist; acquired the 2120 S. Michigan building from the Chess family in 1980 and reequipped the second floor as a working studio.

entities.notes: Via Nadine Cohodas's Spinning Blues into Gold, as reported by the Memphis Flyer.
entities.one_line: Memphis record presser (Plastic Products Company) who suggested the Chess brothers name their label 'Chess.'
Willie Dixon's publishing company founded with proceeds of the 1977 settlement against Arc Music.
Pianist in Muddy Waters's band and core Chess blues session player.
British band named after Muddy Waters's 1950 Chess single 'Rollin' Stone'; recorded at 2120 S. Michigan in June 1964 (12 x 5 sessions), cutting the tribute instrumental '2120 South Michigan Avenue.'
Label founded by Marshall Chess after leaving Chess Records post-GRT.
The 2120 S. Michigan building was designated a Chicago Landmark on May 16, 1990.

entity_registry_notes: canon-chess-records reused from the cross-project audit duplicates.json canonical cluster (BCI-001 b-chess-records + BMI-002 chess-records; BMI-002's 12-claim record was the strongest member). All other IDs are dossier-local, namespaced RD-MUS-000001-###.
